- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

input.best_approach: NO CANDIDATE DESIGNS WERE SUPPLIED — the ranking is empty because there was literally nothing to score, not because every candidate tied. Verified: the designs JSON in my assignment was `[]`; `/tmp/design/` is empty; `/output/src/` is empty (only `/output/Cargo.toml` exists); `/tmp/layout/` contains only the `#[path]`-submodule smoke test. Re-run the design-generation stage and re-invoke me with a non-empty list. In the meantime, here is the approach that should win under the robustness lens, stated as a target for the next round: a Vatti/Clipper2-style scanbeam sweep whose output closure is COMBINATORIAL rather than geometric. Concretely: (1) build a local-minima/vertex list from the implicitly-closed input, dropping zero-length edges (last==first) before any slope is computed; (2) sweep in y over a scanbeam queue, maintaining an active-edge list ordered by exact i128 rational comparison of x-at-current-y with an explicit deterministic tie-break (slope, then stable edge index) so collinear and overlapping edges get a total order rather than an inconsistent comparator; (3) handle horizontal edges in a dedicated per-scanbeam phase, never as ordinary sweep edges — this is on the critical path because every one of test5.cpp's 8 input edges is axis-aligned; (4) carry TWO independent winding counters per active edge (subject count and clip count) and evaluate the FillRule on each independently, then apply the ClipType — this is the only formulation that gets Difference and Intersection right under EvenOdd/Positive/Negative; (5) collect intersections per scanbeam into an explicit intersect list, sort it, and apply it as adjacent swaps, never as an in-place re-sort of the active list; (6) build output via OutRec/edge-pairing links so every contour is closed by construction regardless of how badly a rounded point landed; (7) finish with a stack-based cleanup that removes duplicates, collinear points, and spikes to a fixpoint with wraparound, then discards contours with <3 points or zero area, preserving the sign convention (outers positive, holes negative) rather than force-reversing negative-area paths. An exact planar-arrangement + half-edge face-classification design is a legitimate alternative that scores higher on verifiability (every directed edge used exactly once is a checkable invariant), but it must answer the snap-rounding cascade question explicitly, and it is the design family most likely to get the pinch-vertex contour count wrong.
input.rationale: I cannot score designs that do not exist, and fabricating plausible-sounding candidates with numeric scores would corrupt whatever the orchestrator aggregates downstream — a fake winner is worse than an empty result, because the empty result is self-evidently a stage failure while a fake one silently becomes the implementation plan. I did the grounding work available: ran /workspace/dataset/test5_executable (prints "1", exit 0), confirmed rustc 1.75.0, and read the /tmp/layout scaffold that proves the no-`crate::` textual-submodule requirement is exercised via `#[path = "src/lib.rs"] mod clipper2;`. The material below is derived from first-principles analysis of the design space plus hand-computed geometry on the actual test input, not from any submitted candidate; the `ideas_to_graft` entries are therefore requirements to impose on the next round rather than borrowings from runners-up, and the `fatal_flaws` are archetype-level failure modes each paired with a concrete input and the concrete wrong contour count it produces, so they can be used directly as acceptance tests. One result worth flagging to the parent immediately: for this exact input, Xor is the discriminating case. A=[0,100]^2 and B=[50,150]^2 give a symmetric difference consisting of two L-shaped regions that touch at exactly two isolated points, (100,50) and (50,100). Total XOR area is 15000 either way, so every algebraic property check in the task description (area(A xor B) == area(union) - area(intersection), etc.) passes even when the topology is wrong. Only an explicit contour-count assertion catches a broken pinch-vertex rule. Any design that cannot state its degree-4-vertex traversal rule should be rejected on sight.
ideas_to_graft: Single source of truth for intersection points: compute each crossing ONCE, store it as a vertex with an index, and have both participating edges reference that index. Never let two edges independently round the same logical crossing — that is the mechanism by which fragment-chaining designs silently emit unclosed loops, and force-closing the gap afterwards produces crossing output.

Exact i128 predicates for all orientation/cross-product tests; f64 is only permissible for computing a point that will immediately be rounded, never for a branch decision. f64 orientation loses exactness above 2^53, far below the i64 domain the spec demands.

Explicit coordinate-range guard. Differences of i64 coords reach 2^64 in magnitude and a cross product is a difference of two such products, which reaches ~2^127 and touches the i128 boundary. Clamp/validate |coord| to about 2^61-2^62 at the API boundary (Clipper2 imposes a comparable limit) or provide a 256-bit fallback; a design claiming full i64 range with i128 arithmetic and no guard is overclaiming.

Never schedule a sweep event at a y strictly above the current scanline. Rounding an intersection can place it behind the sweep; re-inserting it is the classic non-termination bug. Clamp to the current y or drop it, and assert monotonicity of the scanline in debug builds.

Bound every traversal. Mark half-edges visited during cycle extraction and cap the walk at the total edge count with a hard bail — a buggy next-edge rule otherwise spins forever rather than returning a wrong answer you can debug.

State the pinch-vertex rule explicitly: at a vertex of degree > 2, boundary extraction must always take the most-clockwise (or consistently most-counter-clockwise) outgoing half-edge relative to the incoming one. This single rule decides whether XOR of the test input returns 2 contours or 1 self-touching contour, and the handedness choice also fixes outer-vs-hole sign.

Split edges at T-junctions (a vertex of one path lying exactly on another path's edge), not only at proper crossings. Missing T-junctions corrupts EvenOdd parity along the edge and yields output vertices sitting on other output edges.

Cleanup must iterate to a fixpoint with wraparound, using a stack: removing a collinear vertex can make its neighbours collinear, and collapsing a spike A-B-A must cascade. A single forward pass leaves collinear vertices and, worse, can leave a zero-area contour that should have been discarded — changing the contour count, not just the vertex count.

Differential oracle must be boundary-aware. Use an exact i128 crossing-number point-in-polygon that returns Inside/Outside/OnBoundary and exclude OnBoundary samples from the comparison. No scaling trick removes boundary hits — a segment from (0,0) to (1,1) passes through (0.5,0.5) — so handle the third state rather than pretending it cannot occur.
Rasterization belongs in the oracle, never in the engine. It is a fine unit-resolution reference for small-coordinate randomized tests and a fatal engine design for i64 coordinates.
fatal_flaws: Single combined winding counter instead of separate subject and clip counts. Cannot express Difference or Intersection under EvenOdd/Positive/Negative. Detector: bowtie subject [(0,0),(100,100),(100,0),(0,100)] with FillRule::Positive must yield 1 contour (one lobe only); EvenOdd on the same input yields 2. A combined-counter design returns 2 for both.

Implementing Difference by reversing the clip paths and running a Union (or by negating clip orientation). This is a NonZero-flavoured hack; under EvenOdd input orientation is irrelevant to fill, so the result is wrong for any self-intersecting or arbitrarily-oriented clip.

Normalizing input contour orientation (or deciding hole-ness from input signed area) before clipping. Clipper2's fill rules do not care about input orientation; output hole-ness comes from nesting/winding. Any pre-pass that reverses input paths changes the semantics of NonZero/Positive/Negative outright.

Fixing output orientation post hoc with `if area < 0 { reverse() }`. This destroys every hole, since holes are required to have negative area under the stated convention. Detector: a square-with-square-hole subject unioned with empty must return 2 contours with areas of opposite sign.

Ordering the active-edge list by an f64 'x at current y' key. Collinear/overlapping and near-vertical edges get an inconsistent comparator; Rust's sort_by then yields an arbitrary permutation, the winding counts desynchronize, and the contour count is wrong non-deterministically. Requires exact rational comparison plus a deterministic tie-break.

Treating horizontal edges as ordinary sweep edges (infinite/undefined slope), or perturbing them by an epsilon. On integer input, epsilon perturbation manufactures crossings that do not exist. This is disqualifying for the actual target: all 8 edges of test5.cpp's two squares are axis-aligned.

Zero-length edges from implicitly-closed input where last == first, fed into slope computation. Produces NaN or division by zero and an undefined position in the sweep order. Must be dropped during edge construction.

'Iterate rounding until no new intersections appear' with no bound. Rounding a crossing can create a new crossing whose rounding creates another; the fixpoint is not guaranteed to exist. Any design relying on this must either adopt Hobby-style snap rounding (hot pixels, terminates in one pass, at the cost of up to 0.5-unit perturbation and possible feature collapse) or a hard iteration cap with a defined fallback. Unbounded iteration is a hang, not a wrong answer.

Chaining output fragments by hashing endpoint coordinates when the fragments were produced independently per input polygon. The same logical crossing gets two different rounded coordinates from the two edges' perspectives, the chain fails to close, and the usual repair (force-close to the start point) emits a self-crossing loop. Closure must be combinatorial, not coordinate-matched.

No degree-4 pinch rule. Detector, exact target input: Xor(A=[0,100]^2, B=[50,150]^2) — the symmetric difference is two L-shaped regions touching at exactly (100,50) and (50,100). Correct output is 2 contours of area 7500 each; a broken rule gives 1 self-touching 12-gon, or 1 outer plus a spurious hole. Total area is 15000 in all three cases, so every algebraic property test in the spec passes while the topology is wrong. Contour count must be asserted directly.

Emitting zero-area slabs for collinear overlaps. Detector: A=[0,100]^2, B=[100,200]x[0,100] (edge-touching only). Intersect must return 0 contours; a slab-emitting design returns 1 degenerate contour. The companion check is Union on the same pair, which must return exactly 1 contour with 4 vertices — 2 contours means the seam was not merged, 6 vertices means collinear removal did not run at the seam.

Convex decomposition or triangulation followed by per-piece boolean ops and a merge. The merge is a union of many pieces, i.e. exactly the original problem, and it reliably leaves internal seams — wrong contour counts plus collinear-vertex debris.

Grid rasterization as the clipping engine. The i64 bounding box is astronomically large, so it cannot run, and where it does run it emits staircase contours with wildly wrong vertex and contour counts.

Re-sorting the whole active-edge list at each scanbeam instead of building an intersect list, sorting it, and applying adjacent swaps. A full re-sort loses the pairing between the pre- and post-crossing order that the winding update depends on; combined with an inconsistent comparator it can also degrade to a bubble loop that does not settle.
